questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Please explain: *
Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I learned French in school and has visited France multiple times. I wanted to improve my language skills while experiencing a new culture and a different health care system

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer:
The Erasmus coordinator was very nice, and helpful throughout the stay. 

It was difficult with the hospital in the beginning. Not much information from the department, I had my clinical rotation at. Luckily I started with other Erasmus and local students. I would highly recommend following the rotation dates of the local students, since you will be able to join the planning of their stay and their courses at the hospital.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I didn't receive any assistance. I had to figure out a lot on my own. But people were very happy to help, when asked.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: I found an apartment through Paris Attitude, which was more expensive, but also with more security.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: It is really nice to live in the city where you are close to everything and you get much more of a feel of the daily life of the locals.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: I needed to apply for Sorbonne Université through their own site and also register for a clinical rotation at the hospital department. Many steps an documents needed (including CV, cover letter etc.), but otherwise quite smooth process. Be prepared, they can be quite slow in sending the necessary documents and information. I only received information about when and where my rotation would take place 1,5 month before I was to begin.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: The Erasmus coordinators from both the University of Copenhagen and Sorbonne Université are available to help via mail.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I did not have any classes. I had to prioritize which department I wanted to do my clinical rotation at. I got my number one priority.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Be patient. In the end everything works out.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: MA

questions.answer: I did not take any courses

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
At the hospital many things are more old fashioned than I was used to. Rounds were done in a big group with several doctors and nurses. Many things were still on paper (the patients were expected to keep all their own documents from previous lab work and hospitalizations).
The students were expected to have obligatory 24h shifts, and 8-18 shifts. All other days were 8-12, since the local students have theoretical classes at the university in the afternoon.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: Not enrolled in any courses. I had my clinical rotation at a department of gynaecology and obstetrics.

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your second semester. *
What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Be aware that English friendly department does not mean that everyone speaks English. They will expect you to speak French.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Go to the smaller cities around Paris. Disneyland is a great theme park (albeit an expensive one)

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: The initial learning curve for me was very steep. My French improved a lot and fast during the stay.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Start your rotation at the same time as them!

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: There can be a lot of paperwork and necessary steps in order to get things done. They can take time, but in the end it usually works out.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The locals take their time to enjoy things. Not everything has to be fast paced.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Go for it! 
The Erasmus coordinators are very nice (and speak English) and want to help.
Be prepared for an immersive language experience - they talk fast, but don't be afraid to tell them that you don't understand.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Be prepared for long processes and early deadlines (both for the university and for grants).

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Feeling that my French improved to a point where the locals would stop changing to English. Being able to enjoy the food and culture of the city at a much slower pace than is usually feasible on shorter trips.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: In the beginning not understanding the language as well and feeling very stupid, when having to ask people to repeat multiple times.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
